games.explanation: Cleveland is the shorter price at home against a Detroit team that is simply better across the board, and the market keeps treating this rivalry like a coin flip because the uniforms look familiar. Bibee's surface numbers are fine until you notice righties are slugging him around whenever they square him up, and Detroit runs Torres, Dingler, and Greene through the top of the order to do exactly that. A hot night with the wind blowing out in a park that already plays hot only sweetens the pot for the lineup that hits the ball harder. Getting the better team at -120 in a spot the sim sees as a genuine edge is the entire ballgame.

Betting against Paul Skenes feels wrong until you remember the other side of the ticket is also getting a decent arm, and the sim spits out a coin flip that the market has decided is a Pittsburgh coronation. Skenes is elite, obviously, but he's noticeably more mortal against righties than lefties, and Miami runs a top-of-order that leans right and puts the ball in play. Eury Perez brings comparable strikeout stuff, meaning this projects as the low-scoring grind where one swing decides everything, exactly the environment where a plus-money dog cashes more than the board suggests. At +106 on a game the numbers call 56/44, you're getting paid to take the better price in a genuine toss-up.

Bryan Woo's numbers look great until you notice which side of the platoon is doing the work, and the Yankees are about to send him a lineup card full of the exact bats his splits don't want to see. Woo has been meaningfully softer against lefties, and Grisham, Rice, and García Jr. are all left-handed hitters producing like middle-of-the-order pieces against right-handed pitching. Rice in particular is sitting on a .412 xwOBA against righties, which is the kind of number that turns a command start into a bullpen game in a hurry. Weathers isn't a strength, but he doesn't have to be when the offense is this well built for the opponent. At -126, you're getting the better team at a price that still treats this like a coin flip.

The market is treating Cease like an ace on reputation, but the underlying profile is a strikeout arm who walks lefties at an alarming clip and gives up loud contact when he doesn't miss bats. Boston happens to be built to exploit exactly that, with Abreu and a lefty-heavy top of the order that can turn Cease's 12% walk rate against southpaws into free baserunners. Contreras is the swing piece, a right-handed bat with barrel-rate juice that plays up against a pitcher whose command wobbles once the whiffs stop coming. Add in Boston being the higher-rated team on the Elo sheet, and getting plus money on the better club against a volatile starter is the entire angle. +137 on the favorite in disguise.

Sanchez is the kind of arm the market reflexively prices as untouchable, but the platoon split tells a different story once you notice the Cardinals send a wave of right-handed bats to the plate. Herrera in particular is the wrong hitter to hand a lefty, and Burleson and Walker do their damage from that same side. Pallante is nobody's idea of an ace, but a 99-degree night with the wind blowing straight in is exactly the environment that flattens the Phillies' slug-first lineup into something manageable. At +152, you're getting a genuine coin flip priced like a 40 percent dog, which is the entire reason to be here.

Snell at plus money against him is a fine idea until you notice the price on the other side, which treats Kansas City like a Triple-A callup instead of a team with a top-of-the-order star who happens to be one of the best lefty-mashers alive. Bobby Witt Jr. has hit lefties even harder than righties this year, and Perez plus Caglianone give Snell enough traffic to worry about the walks he still hands out at a double-digit clip to left-handed pitching's usual counter-lineup. Wacha isn't going to dazzle, but Dodger Stadium in warm crosswind air plays kinder to contact than to Snell's whiff rate, and the sim has this landing inside a run. At +230 on a game the market is pricing closer to 70/30, you only need this to be a coin flip a third of the time.

Getting -115 on a Washington team that only needs to lose close is the kind of price that ages well.

Tampa Bay is the better team, sure, but the market has this priced like the Athletics can't hang around for nine innings, and that's the part worth attacking. Nick Martinez is a soft-contact righty who lives in the zone, which is exactly the profile Soderstrom and the lefty bats in this order tend to punish rather than roll over against. Barnett walks too many people to be efficient, but the sim still lands on a one-run game because Oakland's top four don't have a single automatic out for a pitcher without swing-and-miss stuff. A run and a half at -115 when the projected margin is a tenth of a run is the whole pitch.

Houston is the better team and Hunter Brown is the better arm, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion to give away in a game the sim sees ending inside a single run. Whisenhunt is a mess on paper, yet Daikin Park's suppressed run environment keeps the ceiling on any Astros crooked number, and Brown has been noticeably more hittable against lefties than righties. San Francisco also happens to bring the game's scariest left-handed bat in Devers, who's been abusing right-handed pitching to the tune of a .391 xwOBA. You're getting plus money on a one-run projection, which is the entire trade.
